The inlet Mach number is 2.0 and the Reynolds number based on inlet velocity and axial blade chord is 200,000.
For the adiabatic wall case, the time-averaged characteristic length of the suction side separation bubble is 0.16 axial chord.
For the cooled wall case, the time-averaged characteristic length of the suction side separation bubble is 0.10 axial chord.
The separation bubble is displaced downstream for the cooled wall case compared to the adiabatic case.
The cooled wall case shows a steeper variation in the pressure coefficient downstream of the incident shock.
The wall-normal Reynolds stresses are higher for the adiabatic wall case compared to the cooled wall case.
The grid resolution in wall units for the adiabatic wall case ranges from 6 < Δs+ < 25, 0.1 < Δn+ < 0.3, and 3 < Δz+ < 9.
The grid resolution in wall units for the cooled wall case ranges from 15 < Δs+ < 60, 0.2 < Δn+ < 0.6, and 6 < Δz+ < 19.
The separation and reattachment points of the suction side separation bubble exhibit a breathing pattern of contraction and expansion.
The peak turbulent kinetic energy values are displaced downstream for the cooled wall case compared to the adiabatic case.
The shear layer downstream of the separation bubble is more diffused for the adiabatic case, while more concentrated vorticity values are observed for the cooled wall case.
For the adiabatic wall case, the aerodynamic heating from the surrounding shear layer is transferred into the separation bubble, leading to higher temperatures within the bubble.
Wall cooling induces the formation of a thinner boundary layer, and the sonic line forms closer to the wall for the cooled wall case.
The tangential Reynolds stress distributions reach maximum values just upstream of the shock-bubble interactions, and are similar for both the adiabatic and isothermal walls.
The wall-normal Reynolds stresses reach maximum amplitudes downstream of the shock-boundary layer interaction and are more pronounced for the adiabatic wall.
